ToolFlood: Beyond Selection — Hiding Valid Tools
from LLM Agents via Semantic Covering

Hussein Jawad Affiliation: Capgemini Invent, Paris, France Correspondence to: hussein.jawad@capgemini.com    Nicolas J-B. Brunel Affiliation: Capgemini Invent, Paris, France Affiliation: LaMME, University Paris-Saclay, Evry, France Affiliation: ENSIIE, Evry, France Correspondence to: nicolas.brunel@universite-paris-saclay.fr
Abstract

Large Language Model (LLM) agents increasingly use external tools for complex tasks and rely on embedding-based retrieval to select a small top-kk subset for reasoning. As these systems scale, the robustness of this retrieval stage is underexplored, even though prior work has examined attacks on tool selection. This paper introduces ToolFlood, a retrieval-layer attack on tool-augmented LLM agents. Rather than altering which tool is chosen after retrieval, ToolFlood overwhelms retrieval itself by injecting a few attacker-controlled tools whose metadata is carefully placed by exploiting the geometry of embedding space. These tools semantically span many user queries, dominate the top-kk results, and push all benign tools out of the agent’s context.

ToolFlood uses a two-phase adversarial tool generation strategy. It first samples subsets of target queries and uses an LLM to iteratively generate diverse tool names and descriptions. It then runs an iterative greedy selection that chooses tools maximizing coverage of remaining queries in embedding space under a cosine-distance threshold, stopping when all queries are covered or a budget is reached. We provide theoretical analysis of retrieval saturation and show on standard benchmarks that ToolFlood achieves up to a 95% attack success rate with a low injection rate (1% in ToolBench). The code will be made publicly available at the following link: https://github.com/as1-prog/ToolFlood

Keywords: 
Machine Learning, ICML

1 Introduction

1.1 Scaling Agentic Systems Through Tool Retrieval

The transition from static language models to agentic systems has been driven by the integration of external tools—such as APIs, databases, search engines, and code interpreters—that allow large language models (LLMs) to interact with the external world. Systems such as Toolformer (Schick et al., 2023) and Gorilla (Patil et al., 2023) demonstrate that LLMs can learn to invoke these interfaces via zero-shot or few-shot reasoning, enabling capabilities that are difficult to encode solely within model parameters.

As tool ecosystems expand, discovery becomes a central challenge. Tool distribution platforms like OpenAI GPT Store and LangChain Hub (OpenAI, 2024; LangChain, 2023)—lower the barrier to publishing new tools, rapidly increasing the number and diversity of available capabilities. However, limited context windows make it impractical to present all tools to an agent.

A common solution is tool retrieval: given a user query, the system embeds the query and tool metadata (e.g., name, description, schema) and retrieves the top-kk most relevant tools using dense or hybrid retrieval methods. The agent then performs final selection and planning over this subset. Recent work shows that retrieval quality strongly determines end-to-end agent performance.

1.2 Top-k Domination as a Retrieval-Layer Security Boundary

Prior work on tool-ecosystem attacks has primarily focused on the selection stage: once a malicious tool has already been retrieved and made visible to the agent, the attacker seeks to increase the probability that it is chosen. This is typically achieved by manipulating tool names or descriptions to make malicious tools appear more relevant or attractive (Shi and others, 2025; Mo et al., 2025; Sneh et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025). A central limitation of this line of work is its implicit assumption of a relatively stable candidate set—benign tools remain present in the top-kk list, and the attacker merely competes within that list by promoting one or a small number of malicious tools over nearby benign alternatives.

We identify a distinct failure mode with a different objective and threat model: Top-kk domination. Rather than competing for selection among visible candidates, an adversary aims to control the retrieval context itself by forcing attacker-controlled tools to occupy the entire top-kk list. This reframes the attack from “choose my tool” to “hide all other tools,” constituting a retrieval-stage denial-of-service on tool visibility that can suppress benign tools at the ecosystem level (Zou et al., 2025; Xue et al., 2024).

Crucially, this paradigm renders many existing defenses ineffective. Selection-time mitigations (e.g., prompt-injection filtering or tool-call sanitization) presuppose that benign tools are present in the candidate set (Shi and others, 2025; Wen et al., 2025). Under Top-kk domination, benign tools are never retrieved, and thus selection-time safeguards cannot recover them. The agent is instead forced to reason over an attacker-curated tool universe. This exposes a previously underexplored vulnerability: compromised availability and integrity at the retrieval layer (Zou et al., 2025; Xue et al., 2024).

1.3 ToolFlood: Saturating Top-kk Retrieval with Sybil Swarms

We introduce ToolFlood, a retrieval-layer attack that exploits the geometry of embedding-based tool discovery. ToolFlood injects a Sybil swarm of attacker-controlled tools whose metadata is strategically positioned in embedding space to dominate top-k retrieval results across diverse queries.

ToolFlood operates in two phases. First, it repeatedly samples subsets of target queries and uses an LLM to generate diverse candidate tool names and descriptions tailored to those subsets. Second, it applies a greedy selection process that iteratively chooses tools maximizing coverage of remaining queries in embedding space under a cosine-similarity threshold. This continues until queries are sufficiently covered or a tool budget is exhausted, yielding systematic suppression of benign tools from retrieval.

1.4 Contributions

We summarize our main contributions as follows:

  • •

    Retrieval-layer threat model for tool ecosystems. We identify Top-kk domination as a retrieval-stage attack in which adversaries suppress benign tools by overwhelming the candidate set before tool selection.

  • •

    ToolFlood: semantic covering via Sybil tool swarms. We introduce ToolFlood, an attack that injects strategically embedded tools to saturate top-kk retrieval using LLM-assisted generation and greedy coverage optimization.

  • •

    Theoretical insight into retrieval saturation. We present a geometric analysis showing that a number of injected tools can dominate retrieval by covering the query embedding space under similarity constraints.

  • •

    Empirical evaluation at small poisoning rates. We empirically show that ToolFlood achieves up to 95% top-kk domination with approximately 1%1\% injected tools, exposing the fragility of embedding-based tool discovery.

2 Related Work

2.1 Agent Design Patterns and Tool Ecosystems

The shift from standalone large language models to tool-augmented AI agents is driven by paradigms that combine reasoning with external actions, as well as modular architectures that explicitly route subproblems to specialized components (Karpas et al., 2022).

ReAct (Reasoning + Acting) (Yao et al., 2022) is a prompting technique that enables LLMs to interleave logical reasoning with action execution to solve multi-step problems. Tools are provided to the model via the system prompt as structured definitions (often JSON) that outline their purpose and required parameters. Related systems demonstrate this paradigm in concrete environments, e.g., browser-based question answering (Nakano et al., 2021) and grounded robot planning (Ahn et al., 2022).

Toolformer (Schick et al., 2023) instead learns tool usage through self-supervised fine-tuning, reducing reliance on prompt engineering. As tool ecosystems grew, models like Gorilla (Patil et al., 2023) and ToolLLM (Qin et al., 2024) emerged to handle large and diverse API sets. These approaches rely on retrieval mechanisms to dynamically select relevant tools from large collections based on the user instruction, and condition the model’s reasoning on the retrieved tool descriptions. Beyond one-shot tool use, agent frameworks that incorporate feedback and self-correction (e.g., reflection-based memory) can further improve tool-use performance across trials (Shinn et al., 2023).

2.2 Tool-Specific Attacks

Tool-augmented agents expose attack surfaces beyond the user prompt: tool catalogs (including names, descriptions, and schemas), tool outputs, and orchestration logic can all function as adversarial inputs (Greshake et al., 2023; Zhan et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024).

A first line of work targets tool selection by poisoning or optimizing tool metadata so that malicious tools are preferentially chosen when included in the agent’s context. For example, ToolHijacker (Shi and others, 2025) poisons tool metadata to bias retrieval and selection toward an attacker-controlled tool for a specific task, typically via prompt-injection–style descriptions. Similarly, the Attractive Metadata Attack (AMA) (Mo et al., 2025) shows that syntactically valid and seemingly benign tool descriptions can be iteratively optimized to increase invocation frequency and induce privacy leakage, even under structured tool-calling protocols. Related attacks further demonstrate that small, systematic edits to tool text can bias selection, including black-box perturbation-style attacks (Chen et al., 2025) and iterative description manipulation (Sneh et al., 2025).

A key limitation shared by these approaches is their reliance on competition within the retrieved candidate set. The attacker implicitly assumes that benign tools remain present and visible in a fixed or bounded top-k list, and success depends on outperforming those benign tools during selection. As a result, these attacks can be partially mitigated by prompt-level defenses, post-retrieval filtering or heuristics that downweight overly generic or instruction-like tool descriptions. Moreover, despite being framed as black-box attacks, these methods are not fully model-agnostic. In practice, they rely on shadow retrievers and shadow LLMs to optimize malicious tool metadata and assume sufficient transferability to the target agent. As shown in ToolHijacker, mismatches between the shadow and target LLM architectures or alignment regimes can degrade attack success rates.

In contrast, our work targets the retrieval boundary directly and is model-agnostic with respect to the target LLM agent. ToolFlood achieves top-kk domination through semantic covering, excluding benign tools from the candidate set and thereby converting retrieval into a denial-of-visibility layer.

2.3 Corpus Poisoning and Retrieval Security

A complementary line of work studies retrieval-layer attacks where adversaries compromise a system by manipulating what gets retrieved—either by poisoning the corpus/knowledge base or by subverting the retriever itself. In Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), attackers can inject a small number of crafted passages that are highly retrievable for targeted queries, thereby steering downstream generation toward attacker-chosen outputs (e.g., knowledge corruption and retrieval backdoors) (Zou et al., 2025; Xue et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025a; Shao et al., 2025).

In response, researchers have begun treating the retriever+index as a first-class security boundary, proposing detection and forensic tooling to identify poisoned documents or instruction-bearing context (Tan et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b; Wen et al., 2025). These results motivate our focus on retrieval security in tool-augmented agents: compromising the retrieval set can bypass downstream selection safeguards, manipulating tool retrieval rather than the LLM core.

2.4 Sybil Attacks.

ToolFlood is also closely related to the classical notion of a Sybil attack, where a single adversary creates many pseudo-identities to gain disproportionate influence over a distributed system’s outcomes (e.g., voting, ranking, reputation, or resource allocation) (Douceur, 2002). In open tool hubs and agent tool marketplaces, publishing many near-duplicate tools (or tool “identities”) can similarly skew retrieval and ranking mechanisms—making ToolFlood naturally interpretable as a Sybil-style influence operation against the tool retrieval layer.

3 Formalization

We formalize the end-to-end agent pipeline and the Top-kk domination objective targeted by ToolFlood. The attacker’s goal is to compromise the retrieval boundary by saturating the retriever’s candidate set with attacker-controlled tools, thereby suppressing benign tools and constraining downstream decision-making.

3.1 Agent pipeline

We model the deployed system as a tool-augmented agent that, at each step, maps a natural-language instruction (or intermediate sub-goal) q∈𝒬q\in\mathcal{Q} to either (i) a tool invocation or (ii) a direct natural-language response.

Tool catalog.

Let 𝒯\mathcal{T} be the available tool catalog. Each tool t∈𝒯t\in\mathcal{T} is described by metadata mt∈ℳm_{t}\in\mathcal{M} (e.g., name, description), where ℳ\mathcal{M} denotes the space of metadata strings consumed by the retriever.

Retrieval.

Given a query qq, the retriever embeds the query and each tool’s metadata into a shared dd-dimensional representation space via an embedding function ϕ:𝒬∪ℳ→ℝd\phi:\mathcal{Q}\cup\mathcal{M}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d}. A similarity function s:ℝd×ℝd→ℝs:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} (e.g., cosine similarity) scores the relevance between the embedded query and each tool.

The retriever returns the set Rk​(q,𝒯)R_{k}(q;\mathcal{T}), defined as the top-kk tools with the highest similarity scores:

Rk​(q,𝒯)={t∈𝒯∣s⁡(ϕ⁡(q),ϕ⁡(mt))≥s(k)}.R_{k}(q;\mathcal{T})=\{\,t\in\mathcal{T}\mid s(\phi(q),\phi(m_{t}))\geq s_{(k)}\,\}. (1)

where s(k)s_{(k)} denote the kk-th largest similarity score over 𝒯\mathcal{T}.

Tool selection and arguments.

Conditioned on the query and a set of retrieved candidates CC, the language model policy π\pi selects either a tool t^∈C\hat{t}\in C or abstains (t^=∅\hat{t}=\varnothing). If a tool is selected, π\pi also generates tool arguments a^\hat{a} compatible with the tool interface:

(t^,a^)∼π(⋅∣q,C),t^∈C∪{∅}.(\hat{t},\hat{a})\sim\pi(\cdot\mid q,C),\qquad\hat{t}\in C\cup\{\varnothing\}.

If t^=∅\hat{t}=\varnothing, the agent outputs a natural-language response; otherwise, it invokes t^\hat{t} with arguments a^\hat{a}.

Execution and iteration.

When a tool is invoked, an executor returns an observation oo (tool output), which may be appended to the agent state. Agents may run for multiple steps, but each step follows the same three-stage pattern: Query →\rightarrow Retrieval →\rightarrow Tool Selection (and argument generation).

3.2 Threat Model

Let 𝒯ben\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ben}} denote the benign tool catalog. The attacker injects a set of adversarial tools 𝒯adv\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{adv}}, yielding the deployed catalog

𝒯=𝒯ben∪𝒯adv,|𝒯adv|≤B.\mathcal{T}=\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ben}}\cup\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{adv}},\quad|\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{adv}}|\leq B. (2)

The attacker’s control is restricted to the metadata of injected tools (e.g., name/description/schema), meaning it controls a list of adversarial metadata

ℳadv={m(1),…,m(|𝒯adv|)}.\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{adv}}=\{m^{(1)},\ldots,m^{(|\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{adv}}|)}\}. (3)

Attacker capabilities and limitations.

The attacker cannot modify the retriever RkR_{k}, the embedding function ϕ\phi, the similarity function s⁡(⋅,⋅)s(\cdot,\cdot), nor the agent policies. Their only degree of freedom is selecting the injected tools’ metadata.

Knowledge regimes.

We consider the attacker has no access to the deployed retriever (neither ϕ\phi nor RkR_{k}) and cannot observe retrieval outputs. Instead, they rely on a surrogate (“shadow”) embedding model ϕ~\tilde{\phi} to approximate the geometry of the target embedding space.

3.3 Geometric Formulation: Semantic Covering

To enter the retrieved set Rk​(q,T)R_{k}(q;T), an injected tool’s metadata must be semantically closer to the query qq than benign alternatives in embedding space. We formalize this requirement via semantic covering.

Let ϕ~\tilde{\phi} denote the attacker’s surrogate embedding model (used for geometric reasoning in the black-box regime). Assume all embeddings are ℓ2\ell_{2}-normalized, and define cosine distance as dcos​(u,v)= 1−⟨u,v⟩.d_{\cos}(u,v)\;=\;1-\langle u,v\rangle.

Semantic cover indicator.

For a metadata string m∈ℳm\in\mathcal{M}, a query q∈𝒬q\in\mathcal{Q}, and δ>0\delta>0, we introduce the function

Coverδ(q,m)=[dcos(ϕ~(q),ϕ~(m))≤δ].\operatorname{Cover}^{\delta}(q,m)\;=\;\mathbf{1}\!\left[d_{\cos}\!\big(\tilde{\phi}(q),\tilde{\phi}(m)\big)\leq\delta\right]. (4)

We say that mm covers qq at threshold δ\delta iff Coverδ⁡(q,m)=1\operatorname{Cover}^{\delta}(q,m)=1.

3.4 Optimization Objective: Budgeted Multi-Cover

The attacker’s goal is to construct a set of adversarial tool metadata ℳadv\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{adv}} of size at most BB such that, for queries drawn from the target set 𝒬t​a​r\mathcal{Q}_{tar}, benign tools are suppressed from the retriever’s top-kk results. This requires reaching high density: for each query qq, there should exist multiple adversarial tools whose metadata embeddings lie sufficiently close to the query embedding so that adversarial tools can occupy the top-kk slots.

In order to reach full top-kk domination, the attacker has to choose and optimize the following set

ℳadv\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{adv}} ={m(1),…,m(|𝒯adv|)},\displaystyle=\{m^{(1)},\ldots,m^{(|\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{adv}}|)}\}, (5)

Using the semantic cover indicator (sec.3.3) , we define the adversarial coverage count of a query qq under ℳa​d​v\mathcal{M}_{adv} as

N⁡(q,ℳadv)=∑m∈ℳadvCoverδ​(q,m).N(q;\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{adv}})=\sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{adv}}}\mathrm{Cover}^{\delta}(q,m). (6)

The attacker then solves a budgeted semantic multi-cover problem that rewards covering each query up to quota rr:

maxℳadv⊆ℳ\displaystyle\max_{\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{adv}}\subseteq\mathcal{M}}\quad ∑q∈Qtarmin⁡{r,N⁡(q,ℳadv)}\displaystyle\sum_{q\in Q_{\mathrm{tar}}}\min\bigl\{r,\;N(q;\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{adv}})\bigr\} (7)
s.t. |ℳadv|≤B.\displaystyle|\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{adv}}|\leq B.

The truncation min⁡{r,⋅}\min\{r,\cdot\} prevents wasting budget on over-covering queries that are already saturated, encouraging the attacker to distribute tools across the query space. When r=kr=k, achieving N⁡(q,ℳa​d​v)≥kN(q;\mathcal{M}_{adv})\geq k for many qq makes it feasible for adversarial tools to dominate the retriever’s top-kk list, thereby suppressing benign tools from the agent’s context.

3.5 Attack Objectives

We define the success of the attack at two distinct layers: the retrieval layer (intermediate) and the selection layer (end-to-end).

Retrieval Layer: Top-kk Domination.

For a given query qq, let the deployed tool catalog be 𝒯=𝒯ben∪𝒯adv\mathcal{T}=\mathcal{T}_{\text{ben}}\cup\mathcal{T}_{\text{adv}}, and let the retrieved candidate set be C​(q)=Rk​(q,𝒯)C(q)=R_{k}(q;\mathcal{T}). We define the domination count D⁡(q)D(q) as the number of attacker tools present in the top-kk retrieved set:

D⁡(q,𝒯)=|Rk​(q,𝒯)∩𝒯adv|.D(q;\mathcal{T})=\lvert R_{k}(q;\mathcal{T})\cap\mathcal{T}_{\text{adv}}\rvert. (8)

Since the attacker can only modify the metadata of injected tools, we may also write D⁡(q,Madv)D(q;M_{\text{adv}}) to emphasize that dependence (holding benign metadata fixed).

The attacker achieves Top-kk Domination if D⁡(q,𝒯)=kD(q;\mathcal{T})=k, equivalently Rk​(q,𝒯)⊆𝒯advR_{k}(q;\mathcal{T})\subseteq\mathcal{T}_{\text{adv}}. Under this condition, benign tools are completely excluded from the agent’s context, forcing the planner to reason over an attacker-curated tool universe. We define the Top-kk Domination Rate (TDR) over QtarQ_{\text{tar}} of the adversarial tool 𝒯a​d​v\mathcal{T}_{adv} with metadata ℳa​d​v\mathcal{M}_{adv}:

TDR(ℳa​d​v)=1|Qtar|∑q∈Qtar𝕀[D(q;𝒯)=k].\text{TDR}(\mathcal{M}_{adv})=\frac{1}{\lvert Q_{\text{tar}}\rvert}\sum_{q\in Q_{\text{tar}}}\mathbb{I}\!\left[D(q;\mathcal{T})=k\right]. (9)

Selection Layer: End-to-End Compromise.

The ultimate measure of attack success is whether the agent ultimately selects an adversarial tool. Let (t^,a^)∼π(⋅∣q,C(q))(\hat{t},\hat{a})\sim\pi(\cdot\mid q,C(q)) denote the tool (and arguments) chosen by the agent, conditioned on the retrieved candidate set C⁡(q)C(q). We define the Attack Success Rate (ASR) over the target query set QtarQ_{\text{tar}} as

ASR(ℳadv)=1|Qtar|∑q∈Qtar𝔼π[𝕀[t^∈𝒯adv]].\text{ASR}(\mathcal{M}_{\text{adv}})=\frac{1}{\lvert Q_{\text{tar}}\rvert}\sum_{q\in Q_{\text{tar}}}\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\mathbb{I}\!\left[\hat{t}\in\mathcal{T}_{\text{adv}}\right]\right]. (10)

Top-kk domination constitutes a sufficient condition for controlling the selection stage. Specifically, if D⁡(q,𝒯)=kD(q;\mathcal{T})=k, then the retrieved candidate set C⁡(q)C(q) contains only adversarial tools, and the probability of selecting a benign tool is zero. Consequently, if t^≠∅\hat{t}\neq\varnothing, we have

ASR​(ℳadv)≥TDR​(ℳadv),\text{ASR}(\mathcal{M}_{\text{adv}})\geq\text{TDR}(\mathcal{M}_{\text{adv}}),

since adversarial tools may still be selected even when domination is partial (0<D⁡(q,𝒯)<k0<D(q;\mathcal{T})<k).

In our experiments, we set the selection temperature of the target agent to 0, making tool selection deterministic. Under this setting, the expectation over the policy π\pi becomes unnecessary, and ASR reduces to the empirical fraction of queries for which an adversarial tool is selected:

ASR(ℳadv)=1|Qtar|∑q∈Qtar𝕀[t^(q)∈𝒯adv].\text{ASR}(\mathcal{M}_{\text{adv}})=\frac{1}{\lvert Q_{\text{tar}}\rvert}\sum_{q\in Q_{\text{tar}}}\mathbb{I}\!\left[\hat{t}(q)\in\mathcal{T}_{\text{adv}}\right]. (11)

4 Methodology

4.1 Overview

ToolFlood achieves Top-k domination through a two-phase attack strategy. First, it stochastically explores the semantic space of target queries to generate a diverse pool of adversarial tool metadata. Second, it formulates tool injection as a budgeted semantic multi-cover problem and applies a greedy optimization procedure to select a small subset of tools that collectively displace benign tools from the retriever’s top-k results across as many queries as possible.

4.2 Phase 1: Monte Carlo Candidate Generation

The goal of Phase 1 is to generate a diverse and sufficiently large pool of candidate adversarial tools that collectively cover the semantic space of target queries, so later stages have enough “raw material” to dominate top-k retrieval.

Let 𝒬t​a​r\mathcal{Q}_{tar} be the set of target user queries. We execute the following process for II iterations:

  1. 1.

    Subset sampling. Sample a subset Si⊂𝒬tarS_{i}\subset\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{tar}} uniformly at random without replacement, with |Si|=n|S_{i}|=n.

  2. 2.

    Conditional generation. Generate gg tool metadata strings Gi={mi,1,…,mi,g}G_{i}=\{m_{i,1},\dots,m_{i,g}\}, such that mi,j∼ℙA(⋅|Si)m_{i,j}\sim\mathbb{P}^{A}(\cdot|S_{i}). The metadata random generator is typically an attacker-controlled LLM that is asked to generate metadata semantically relevant to all queries in SiS_{i} (rather than tailored to a single query).

Aggregation: The final candidate pool of metadata 𝒫I\mathcal{P}_{I} is simply the union 𝒫I=⋃i=1IGi\mathcal{P}_{I}=\bigcup_{i=1}^{I}G_{i}, which contains I×gI\times g tools.

Motivation: Conditioning on a small set of queries encourages the LLM to generate tool descriptions that sit in the shared region of embedding space for that subset, producing candidates that tend to generalize across multiple nearby queries (useful for multi-cover) rather than creating one-off, query-specific strings.

4.3 Phase 2: Iterative Greedy Semantic Multi-Covering

Given the candidate metadata pool 𝒫I\mathcal{P}_{I} and an injection budget BB, the attacker’s goal is to select a subset ℳadv⊆𝒫I\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{adv}}\subseteq\mathcal{P}_{I} (where |ℳadv|≤B|\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{adv}}|\leq B) that maximizes the number of saturated queries. A query is considered saturated if it is covered by at least rr adversarial tools, where rr is set to the retrieval parameter kk to ensure benign tools are fully displaced.

This formulation corresponds to the Budgeted Maximum Coverage problem, which is NP-hard (Khuller et al., 1999). We employ an iterative greedy approximation (Nemhauser et al., 1978; Khuller et al., 1999).

Initialization.

We initialize the adversarial metadata set ℳadv←∅\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{adv}}\leftarrow\emptyset. For each query q∈Qtarq\in Q_{\text{tar}}, we initialize a coverage counter c⁡(q)←0c(q)\leftarrow 0. We also initialize the residual query set R←QtarR\leftarrow Q_{\text{tar}}.

Procedure.

We repeat the following procedure until either R=∅R=\emptyset or |ℳadv|=B|\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{adv}}|=B:

  1. 1.

    Marginal Gain Computation. For each candidate metadata string m∈𝒫I∖ℳadvm\in\mathcal{P}_{I}\setminus\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{adv}}, compute its marginal coverage gain over the residual queries, using the appropriate coverage function from section 3.3:
    gain​(m)=∑q∈RCoverδ​(q,m).\text{gain}(m)=\sum_{q\in R}\text{Cover}^{\delta}(q,m).

  2. 2.

    Greedy Selection. Select the metadata string with maximum marginal gain: m∗=arg⁡maxm∈𝒫I∖ℳadv​gain​(m)m^{*}=\arg\max_{m\in\mathcal{P}_{I}\setminus\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{adv}}}\text{gain}(m)

  3. 3.

    Early Termination Check. If gain​(m∗)=0\text{gain}(m^{*})=0, terminate early, as no remaining candidate metadata can cover any residual query under the chosen similarity threshold.

  4. 4.

    Update Adversarial Metadata Set. Add the selected metadata string to the adversarial set: ℳadv←ℳadv∪{m∗}.\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{adv}}\leftarrow\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{adv}}\cup\{m^{*}\}.

  5. 5.

    Update Coverage Counts. For each query q∈Rq\in R such that Coverδ​(q,m∗)=1\text{Cover}^{\delta}(q,m^{*})=1:

    • •

      increment c⁡(q)←c⁡(q)+1c(q)\leftarrow c(q)+1;

    • •

      if c⁡(q)≥rc(q)\geq r, remove qq from the residual set RR.

Outcome.

The resulting metadata set ℳadv\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{adv}} defines the injected adversarial tools. Queries that reach coverage r=kr=k empirically tend to have their top-kk retrieval results fully occupied by attacker-controlled tools, thereby excluding all benign tools from the retrieval context.

4.4 Theoretical Guarantees

Although Phase 2 uses a greedy approximation, Phase 1 admits a formal convergence guarantee: with enough randomized subset prompts and generated tools, the candidate pool will contain sufficient “ammunition” to saturate the top-kk retrieval list for all target queries with high probability.

Assumptions.

Let δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1) be a cosine-distance threshold in the surrogate embedding space ϕ~\tilde{\phi}, and let Coverδ​(q,m)\mathrm{Cover}^{\delta}(q,m) be the cover indicator (Eq. 4). We assume the conditional generator ℙA(⋅∣S)\mathbb{P}^{A}(\cdot\mid S) satisfies:

  • •

    (A1) Positive per-appearance coverage probability: For all q∈𝒬tarq\in\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{tar}}, there exists a constant pq>0p_{q}>0 such that for any subset S⊂𝒬tarS\subset\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{tar}} with q∈Sq\in S, if m∼ℙA(⋅∣q∈S)m\sim\mathbb{P}^{A}(\cdot\mid q\in S), then ℙA​(Coverδ​(q,m)=1∣q∈S)≥pq.\mathbb{P}^{A}\!\left(\mathrm{Cover}^{\delta}(q,m)=1\mid q\in S\right)\geq p_{q}.

  • •

    (A2) Independence: Forall i=1,…,I,j=1,…,gi=1,\dots,I,j=1,\dots,g, mi,j∼ℙA(⋅|Si)m_{i,j}\sim\mathbb{P}^{A}(\cdot|S_{i}) are independent.

Choosing δ\delta.

In practice, δ\delta can be set using small quantiles (e.g., 1–5%) of cosine distances under ϕ~\tilde{\phi}, so “covered” means closer than most benign tools in embedding space; an LLM generator with the prompt in Appendix D is used to satisfy (A1).

Theorem 4.1 (Phase 1 Multi-Cover Convergence).

Let 𝒫I\mathcal{P}_{I} be the Phase 1 candidate pool after II iterations, and define N⁡(q,𝒫I)=∑m∈𝒫ICoverδ⁡(q,m).N(q,\mathcal{P}_{I})\;=\;\sum_{m\in\mathcal{P}_{I}}\operatorname{Cover}^{\delta}(q,m). Then:

  1. 1.

    (Per-query convergence) For every target query q∈𝒬t​a​rq\in\mathcal{Q}_{tar}:

    Pr[N(q,𝒫I)≥r]→I→∞1\Pr[N(q,\mathcal{P}_{I})\geq r]\xrightarrow[I\to\infty]{}1 (12)
  2. 2.

    (Uniform convergence) The probability that the entire target set is successfully rr-multi-covered approaches certainty:

    Pr[∀q∈𝒬t​a​r,N(q,𝒫I)≥r]→I→∞1\Pr[\forall q\in\mathcal{Q}_{tar},\,N(q,\mathcal{P}_{I})\geq r]\xrightarrow[I\to\infty]{}1 (13)

This guarantees that, for any finite target set, sufficiently many Phase 1 iterations will produce a pool containing enough candidates to enable full top-kk displacement (given an effective Phase 2 selection). The full proof and detailed assumptions are provided in Appendix C.

5 Experiments

This section evaluates whether ToolFlood achieves top-k domination across realistic tool catalogs and retriever configurations.

5.1 Experimental setup

Agent pipeline.

As formalized in Section 3.1, each evaluation follows a fixed three-stage agent pipeline: Query →\rightarrow Retrieval →\rightarrow Tool Selection. Given a natural-language query qq, the retriever embeds qq together with tool metadata and returns the top-kk candidate tools based on cosine similarity. Then, an LLM selects a tool conditioned on the retrieved candidate set.

Tool Catalogs and Benchmarks.

We evaluate on two benchmark-derived tool ecosystems: MetaTool (Huang et al., 2023) and ToolBench (Guo et al., 2024). Each benchmark consists of a library of benign tool documents (𝒯b​e​n\mathcal{T}_{ben}) containing names, descriptions. MetaTool contains 199 benign tools, while ToolBench contains 11,760 benign tools.

Queries and tasks.

Following the ToolHijacker-style protocol (Shi and others, 2025), we define 10 target tasks 𝒬tar(ℓ),ℓ=1,…,10\mathcal{Q}^{(\ell)}_{\mathrm{tar}},\ell=1,\dots,10 per benchmark and generate 100 semantically varied queries per task (1,000 total), each paired with a ground-truth benign tool. (More details in Appendix E).

To avoid evaluation leakage, we adopt a no-contamination split: a subset QgenQ_{\mathrm{gen}} is used only for ToolFlood’s candidate generation and greedy selection, while a disjoint held-out subset QtestQ_{\mathrm{test}} is used only for final evaluation. In our setup, we report per task |Qgen|=100|Q_{\mathrm{gen}}|=100 and |Qtest|=50|Q_{\mathrm{test}}|=50; unless otherwise stated, all results are computed on QtestQ_{\mathrm{test}}, and metrics are averaged across all tasks when shown.

Retrievers and embeddings.

ToolFlood is optimized using a shadow embedding model ϕ~\tilde{\phi} (a black-box surrogate), while evaluation may use a different target embedding model ϕ\phi. This allows us to measure transferability under matched versus mismatched retrievers. We evaluate using OpenAI text-embedding-3-small and text-embedding-3-large (OpenAI, ; OpenAI, ; OpenAI, ), as well as the Sentence-Transformers all-MiniLM-L6-v2 encoder (sentence-transformers, ).

Deployment Under Attack.

To simulate a compromised marketplace, we deploy an augmented tool library: 𝒯=𝒯b​e​n∪𝒯a​d​v\mathcal{T}=\mathcal{T}_{ben}\cup\mathcal{T}_{adv}, where 𝒯a​d​v\mathcal{T}_{adv} represents the swarm of attacker-controlled tools injected via ToolFlood. We report the normalized poisoning rate P​R≐|𝒯a​d​v|/|𝒯b​e​n|PR\doteq|\mathcal{T}_{adv}|/|\mathcal{T}_{ben}| to account for the significant size difference between the MetaTool and ToolBench catalogs.

5.2 Attack configuration

Unless stated otherwise, ToolFlood uses the following parameters.

Retrieval depth. We set k=5k=5 and target full domination with quota r=kr=k.

Phase 1 (candidate generation). We run I=1000I=1000 iterations. In each iteration, we sample |Si|=20|S_{i}|=20 queries and generate |Gi|=10|G_{i}|=10 candidate tools, yielding a total candidate pool size of 𝒫I=I⋅|Gi|=10000\mathcal{P}_{I}=I\cdot|G_{i}|=10000. For ℙA​(⋅)\mathbb{P}^{A}(\cdot), we use gpt-4o-mini as the attacker-controlled LLM for candidate generation (the prompt template is provided in Appendix D).

Phase 2 (greedy multi-cover). We apply greedy semantic multi-cover selection under a fixed black-box cosine-distance threshold δ=0.3\delta=0.3, which corresponds to the 5% quantile of cosine distances under ϕ~\tilde{\phi} between queries and benign tools in each benchmark. We vary the injection budget BB and report the poisoning rate P​R=|𝒯adv|/|𝒯ben|PR=|\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{adv}}|/|\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ben}}|.

5.3 Baselines

We compare ToolFlood against two retrieval-layer attack baselines that operate under the same tool catalogs, retriever configuration (top-k=5k=5), and evaluation pipeline used throughout our experiments.

Random-Sybil Injection. This baseline models an untargeted Sybil-style flooding attack. An attacker injects a budget BB of tool metadata (name, description) that follow the benign format but are not optimized for any target query distribution QtarQ_{\mathrm{tar}}. No coverage- or similarity-based selection is applied.

PoisonedRAG (adapted for tool poisoning). PoisonedRAG is a retrieval poisoning attack originally designed for RAG systems (Zou et al., 2025). We adapt it by treating each tool’s metadata as a retrievable passage and generating query-targeted poisoned tool metadata.

Concretely, for each target query q∈Qtarq\in Q_{\mathrm{tar}}, we construct a poisoned metadata description m⁡(q)=I⁡(q)⊕S⁡(q)m(q)=I(q)\oplus S(q), where I⁡(q)=qI(q)=q is the literal query text and S⁡(q)S(q) is a single sentence generated by an attacker-controlled LLM (GPT-4o-mini). We enforce semantic proximity by only accepting generations that satisfy dcos​(ϕ~​(q),ϕ~​(S⁡(q)))<0.3d_{\cos}\!\bigl(\tilde{\phi}(q),\tilde{\phi}(S(q))\bigr)<0.3.

Baselines not included. We do not compare against AMA (Mo et al., 2025) or ToolTweak(Sneh et al., 2025) because they primarily target a different regime: the attacker optimizes metadata to win selection among a small, explicitly provided candidate set (i.e., tools are already available in-context, rather than discovered via large-scale retrieval). In particular, ToolTweak evaluates selection among only five tools, which does not reflect the large-catalog retrieval setting considered in this work.

We also exclude ToolHijacker (Shi and others, 2025) from our comparison. Although the paper describes a two-stage retrieval and selection attack with a multi-phase optimization strategy, the repository is not publicly available, and the paper does not provide sufficient implementation details to support a faithful and reproducible reimplementation.

5.4 Main results

Overall effectiveness. As shown in Table 1, ToolFlood consistently achieves strong retrieval-layer domination (TDR) and end-to-end compromise (ASR) across both MetaTool and ToolBench. In the black-box setting, it reaches 97.2% TDR on MetaTool and 91.0% TDR on ToolBench, yielding ∼\sim95–100% ASR across different selector LLMs, while random Sybil flooding remains largely ineffective and PoisonedRAG is generally weaker on ToolBench.

Budget scaling by task. Figure 1 shows that ASR increases monotonically with injection budget across tasks in the black-box ToolBench setting, consistent with the intuition that additional tools improve semantic covering and increase the chance of fully occupying the top-kk list.

5.5 Transferability across retrievers

We test whether ToolFlood optimized on one embedding model transfers to others. Table 2 reports TDR/ASR when varying the target retriever (used for evaluation) and the shadow retriever (used for optimization). ToolFlood remains effective under mismatched settings—for instance, optimizing with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and evaluating on text-embedding-3-small retains substantial performance (TDR =84%=84\%, ASR =91.2%=91.2\%).

5.6 Defense evaluation

We evaluate whether standard retrieval-time defenses mitigate ToolFlood using: (i) Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) (Carbonell and Goldstein, 1998) reranking to promote diversity among the top-kk retrieved tools, and (ii) prompt-attack detection to filter suspicious tool metadata prior to selection. For the latter, we apply Llama Prompt Guard (86M) (Meta AI, 2024; Meta AI, 2025).

Using the same ToolFlood setup as in the main experiments, we evaluate these defenses on ToolBench with GPT-4o-mini as the selector, reporting Top-kk Domination Rate (TDR) and Attack Success Rate (ASR) (Table 3). MMR substantially reduces domination (from 91.0%91.0\% to 44.8%44.8\%); however, ASR remains high (∼91.0%\sim\!91.0\%), indicating that partial flooding is sufficient to steer tool selection. In contrast, Prompt Guard filtering provides no benefit (TDR 91.0%91.0\%, ASR 96.1%96.1\%), consistent with ToolFlood relying on broad semantic coverage rather than explicit instruction-like payloads detectable by prompt-injection defenses (Wen et al., 2025).

6 Discussion and Future Work

Implications.

ToolFlood shifts tool-ecosystem security from competition within a retrieved set to attacks on the retrieval boundary itself. If adversaries can saturate the top-kk list, downstream safeguards are bypassed because benign tools never enter context. This risk is especially salient in open or semi-open tool marketplaces, and aligns tool retrieval with prior findings that retrieval components are a critical security surface in LLM systems, deserving first-class assurance and monitoring.

Limitations.

The attack assumes an adversary can inject or sustain many tools, which may not apply to tightly curated registries. It also relies on surrogate embedding models, so effectiveness may drop as deployed retrievers diverge or incorporate hybrid and learned components. Our evaluation focuses on top-kk saturation under benchmark settings, and does not fully capture interactions with deployment-specific signals or defense-in-depth strategies.

Future Work.

Future work should pursue Sybil-resilient tool retrieval, particularly methods that reduce redundancy and near-duplicate domination. Promising directions include diversity-aware reranking, retrieval-layer anomaly detection for flooding patterns, and stronger provenance and governance mechanisms. Additionally, robust training objectives and adaptive retrieval policies may reduce sensitivity to semantic covering while preserving retrieval utility.

Impact Statement

This paper studies the security of embedding-based tool retrieval in tool-augmented LLM agents, and introduces ToolFlood, a retrieval-layer attack that can saturate top-kk retrieval and thereby hide benign tools from the agent’s context. Such “top-kk domination” effectively turns tool retrieval into a denial-of-visibility mechanism, bypassing selection-time safeguards that assume benign tools remain retrievable.

Potential positive impacts. By characterizing this failure mode and empirically evaluating it, our work can help tool-marketplace operators and agent developers understand an underexplored security boundary and prioritize mitigations. In particular, it may motivate more robust, Sybil-resilient retrieval and governance mechanisms (e.g., diversity-aware reranking, anomaly detection for flooding patterns, and stronger provenance controls) that improve the reliability and trustworthiness of tool-augmented systems in real deployments.

Potential negative impacts and dual-use risk. The techniques described are dual-use: adversaries could exploit similar semantic-covering strategies to suppress legitimate tools in open or semi-open tool ecosystems, potentially causing service disruption, steering agents toward attacker-controlled toolsets, and increasing downstream risks (e.g., erroneous actions or privacy/security incidents) when agents are used in high-stakes settings. To reduce misuse, we emphasize that our contribution is primarily diagnostic—intended to inform defenses and measurement—and we encourage evaluation and red-teaming in controlled environments alongside deployment of retrieval-layer hardening (e.g., redundancy/near-duplicate controls, diversity constraints, rate limits, and monitoring for flooding behaviors).

Overall, we hope this work strengthens the safety and robustness of tool-augmented LLM agents by prompting systematic attention to retrieval-layer integrity and availability.

Appendix B ToolFlood Pseudocode

B.1 Algorithm A1: Phase 1 — Monte Carlo Candidate Generation

Goal: Build a large, diverse pool of candidate adversarial tool metadata by repeatedly sampling query subsets and prompting an LLM to generate tools that are jointly relevant to all queries in each subset.

Inputs: Target queries: QtarQ_{\mathrm{tar}}; iterations: II; subset size: nn; tools generated per iteration: gg; generator: LLMGenerateTools​(S,g)\textsc{LLMGenerateTools}(S,g).

Output: Candidate pool 𝒫\mathcal{P}.

B.2 Algorithm A2: Phase 2 — Iterative Greedy Semantic Multi-Cover

Goal: Select up to budget BB tools from candidate pool 𝒫I\mathcal{P}_{I} to multi-cover as many target queries as possible until each query reaches quota rr (often r=kr=k for full top-kk domination).

Inputs: Target queries: QtarQ_{\mathrm{tar}}; candidate pool: 𝒫\mathcal{P}; coverage quota per query: rr; injection budget: BB; shadow embedding model ϕ~\tilde{\phi}; cosine-distance threshold δ\delta. Coverage is determined by the semantic cover indicator Coverδ⁡(⋅,⋅)\operatorname{Cover}^{\delta}(\cdot,\cdot) defined in Eq. (4)

Output: Selected adversarial metadata set ℳadv\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{adv}}.

B.3 Algorithm A3: ToolFlood — Full Two-Phase Attack (Using A1 and A2)

Goal: Generate candidates (Phase 1), then greedily select a small injected swarm that maximizes semantic multi-cover under budget (Phase 2).

Inputs: Qtar,I,n,gQ_{\mathrm{tar}},I,n,g; coverage quota rr; budget BB; shadow embedding model ϕ~\tilde{\phi}; cosine-distance threshold δ\delta.

Output: 𝒯adv\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{adv}}.

Appendix C Theoretical Insights: Phase-1 Multi-Cover Convergence

This section provides a formal theoretical justification for the Phase 1 Monte Carlo candidate-generation procedure used in ToolFlood. We demonstrate that, under mild assumptions, the repeated randomized subset sampling and conditioned tool generation process is guaranteed to yield an rr-multi-cover of all target queries with high probability as the number of iterations II increases.

C.1 Setup and Notation

Let 𝒬t​a​r\mathcal{Q}_{tar} be the finite set of target queries with cardinality |𝒬t​a​r|=N|\mathcal{Q}_{tar}|=N. The Phase 1 process evolves over iterations i=1,2,…,Ii=1,2,\dots,I as follows:

  1. 1.

    Random Subset Sampling: At each iteration ii, a subset Si⊆𝒬t​a​rS_{i}\subseteq\mathcal{Q}_{tar} of size |Si|=n|S_{i}|=n is sampled uniformly at random without replacement.

  2. 2.

    Conditional Tool Generation: For each sampled subset SiS_{i}, the LLM generates g≥1g\geq 1 candidate tool metadata strings. Let mi,jm_{i,j} denote the metadata of the jj-th tool generated at iteration ii (where 1≤j≤g1\leq j\leq g). The cumulative candidate metadata pool after II iterations is defined as

    𝒫I:=⋃i=1I{mi,1,…,mi,g}.\mathcal{P}_{I}:=\bigcup_{i=1}^{I}\{m_{i,1},\ldots,m_{i,g}\}. (14)
  3. 3.

    Coverage Condition: Let ϕ~​(⋅)\tilde{\phi}(\cdot) be the embedding function and dc​o​s​(⋅,⋅)d_{cos}(\cdot,\cdot) be the cosine distance. A tool tt is said to cover a query qq if their semantic distance falls below the attack-specific threshold:

    Cover​(q,t)⇔dc​o​s​(ϕ~​(q),ϕ~​(mt))≤δ\text{Cover}(q,t)\iff d_{cos}(\tilde{\phi}(q),\tilde{\phi}(m_{t}))\leq\delta (15)

    As in Eq.6, we define N⁡(q,𝒫I)N(q,\mathcal{P}_{I}) as the number of generated tools metadata in 𝒫I\mathcal{P}_{I} that cover query qq.

Sampling Probability:

Let α\alpha denote the probability that a specific query qq is included in the random subset SiS_{i} at any given iteration. For a subset of size nn drawn uniformly from a population of NN:

α:=Pr⁡(q∈Si)=nN\alpha:=\Pr(q\in S_{i})=\frac{n}{N} (16)

C.2 Assumptions

To establish convergence, we rely on two probabilistic assumptions regarding the generator’s behavior:

  • •

    (A1) Positive Conditional Coverage Probability: For every query q∈𝒬t​a​rq\in\mathcal{Q}_{tar}, there exists a constant pq>0p_{q}>0 such that if qq is present in the prompt context (q∈Siq\in S_{i}), any generated tool metadata mi,jm_{i,j} covers qq with probability at least pqp_{q}.

    Pr⁡(Cover​(q,mi,j)∣Si)≥pq\Pr(\text{Cover}(q,m_{i,j})\mid S_{i})\geq p_{q} (17)
  • •

    (A2) Independence: We assume the coverage outcomes of distinct generated tools are independent conditional on the subset SiS_{i}. Formally, the indicator variables for coverage are independent or can be lower-bounded by independent Bernoulli trials.

C.3 Main Result

Theorem C.1 (Phase 1 Multi-Cover Convergence).

Fix a desired coverage quota r≥1r\geq 1. Then:

  1. 1.

    Binomial Lower Bound: For any target query q∈𝒬t​a​rq\in\mathcal{Q}_{tar}, the cumulative coverage count N⁡(q,𝒫I)N(q,\mathcal{P}_{I}) stochastically dominates a Binomial random variable:

    N⁡(q,𝒫I)⪰Binomial​(I⋅g,α⋅pq)N(q,\mathcal{P}_{I})\succeq\text{Binomial}(I\cdot g,\alpha\cdot p_{q}) (18)
  2. 2.

    Per-Query Convergence: For every q∈𝒬t​a​rq\in\mathcal{Q}_{tar}, the probability of achieving the necessary coverage approaches certainty:

    limI→∞Pr[N(q,𝒫I)≥r]=1\lim_{I\to\infty}\Pr[N(q,\mathcal{P}_{I})\geq r]=1 (19)
  3. 3.

    Uniform Convergence: The probability that all queries in the target set are successfully covered by at least rr tools approaches certainty:

    limI→∞Pr[∀q∈𝒬t​a​r,N(q,𝒫I)≥r]=1\lim_{I\to\infty}\Pr[\forall q\in\mathcal{Q}_{tar},N(q,\mathcal{P}_{I})\geq r]=1 (20)

C.4 Proof

Proof.

Step 1: Lower Bounding Single-Trial Probability
Let Xi,j​(q)X_{i,j}(q) be the indicator variable that is 11 if the jj-th tool in iteration ii covers query qq, and 00 otherwise. Using the Law of Total Probability, we derive the unconditional probability of coverage for a single generated tool:

Pr[Xi,j(q)=1]≥Pr[Xi,j(q)=1∣Si]⋅Pr[Si]\Pr[X_{i,j}(q)=1]\geq\Pr[X_{i,j}(q)=1\mid S_{i}]\cdot\Pr[S_{i}] (21)

Substituting our definitions from A.1 and A.2:

Pr[Xi,j(q)=1]≥pq⋅α=n⋅pqN\Pr[X_{i,j}(q)=1]\geq p_{q}\cdot\alpha=\frac{n\cdot p_{q}}{N} (22)

Let μq=n⋅pqN\mu_{q}=\frac{n\cdot p_{q}}{N} denote this effective lower-bound success rate per generation slot.

Step 2: Stochastic Domination
The total coverage count is the sum of these indicators over all iterations and generation slots:

N⁡(q,𝒫I)=∑i=1I∑j=1gXi,j​(q)N(q,\mathcal{P}_{I})=\sum_{i=1}^{I}\sum_{j=1}^{g}X_{i,j}(q) (23)

Under Assumption (A2), this sum of I⋅gI\cdot g Bernoulli trials (each with success probability at least μq\mu_{q}) stochastically dominates a Binomial distribution Z∼Binomial​(I⋅g,μq)Z\sim\text{Binomial}(I\cdot g,\mu_{q}).

Step 3: Convergence via Chernoff Bounds
From Step 2, N⁡(q,𝒫I)N(q,\mathcal{P}_{I}) stochastically dominates a binomial random variable Z∼Binomial⁡(I⋅g,μq)Z\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(I\cdot g,\mu_{q}), i.e.,

Pr[N(q,𝒫I)<r]≤Pr[Z<r].\Pr[N(q,\mathcal{P}_{I})<r]\leq\Pr[Z<r].

Let μ:=𝔼⁡[X]=I⋅g⋅μq\mu:=\mathbb{E}[X]=I\cdot g\cdot\mu_{q}. For all sufficiently large II, we have μ≥r\mu\geq r. Applying the standard Chernoff lower-tail bound in the form

Pr[X≤r]≤exp(−(μ−r)22​μ)(r≤μ),\Pr[X\leq r]\leq\exp\!\left(-\frac{(\mu-r)^{2}}{2\mu}\right)\qquad(r\leq\mu),

we obtain

Pr[N(q,𝒫I)<r]≤exp(−(I⋅g⋅μq−r)22​I⋅g⋅μq).\Pr[N(q,\mathcal{P}_{I})<r]\leq\exp\!\left(-\frac{(I\cdot g\cdot\mu_{q}-r)^{2}}{2\,I\cdot g\cdot\mu_{q}}\right).

As I→∞I\to\infty, the exponent grows on the order of II, so the right-hand side decays exponentially to 00; hence Pr[N(q,𝒫I)≥r]→1\Pr[N(q,\mathcal{P}_{I})\geq r]\to 1.

Step 4: Uniform Convergence
To show that the entire set 𝒬t​a​r\mathcal{Q}_{tar} is covered, we apply Boole’s inequality (Union Bound). The probability that at least one query fails to meet the quota rr is:

Pr[∃q∈𝒬t​a​r:N(q,𝒫I)<r]≤∑q∈𝒬t​a​rPr[N(q,𝒫I)<r]\Pr[\exists q\in\mathcal{Q}_{tar}:N(q,\mathcal{P}_{I})<r]\leq\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_{tar}}\Pr[N(q,\mathcal{P}_{I})<r] (24)

Since 𝒬t​a​r\mathcal{Q}_{tar} is finite (size NN) and each term in the sum goes to 0 as I→∞I\to\infty, the total failure probability vanishes.

limI→∞Pr[minqN(q,𝒫I)≥r]=1\lim_{I\to\infty}\Pr[\min_{q}N(q,\mathcal{P}_{I})\geq r]=1 (25)

Conclusion: This confirms that with a sufficient budget of iterations II, the stochastic exploration in Phase 1 provides sufficient “ammunition” (candidate tools) to saturate the retrieval results for every target query. ∎
